What I can certify

1

What I Can and Cannot Certify

Colorado notary law (RULONA)

Based on Colorado notary law (RULONA) and Colorado Secretary of State guidance.

✔I can certify copies of:

  • Diplomas, degrees and school records (transcripts, certificates of completion).
  • Passports, driver's licenses and ID cards — the photo and data page.
  • Birth, death, marriage or divorce certificates from other states (not Colorado).
  • Records issued outside Colorado, including documents from other countries.
  • Private records you hold in original: contracts, leases, bank statements, letters, medical or business records.

✘I cannot certify:

  • Colorado birth, death, marriage or divorce certificates. Order a certified copy from Colorado Vital Records or your county.
  • Anything you can get from a Colorado county Clerk and Recorder (deeds, recorded documents), the Colorado Secretary of State, or the Colorado State Archives. Ask that office for the certified copy.
  • Documents that say on their face it is illegal to copy them, such as U.S. naturalization and citizenship certificates.
  • That a person is alive ("proof of life", "life certificate", "fe de vida"). A Colorado notary does not certify facts. If the agency accepts it, the person can sign a sworn statement in front of me and I notarize their signature.
  • A copy of a copy, a fax, or a scan. I need to see the original document.

Before the appointment: ask whoever is receiving your document whether they accept a notary-certified copy. That decision is theirs. I don’t give legal or immigration advice.

2

How It Works & What It Costs

  1. 1

    Bring the original. I must see the original record; I cannot certify from another copy.

  2. 2

    I make or supervise the copy and compare it page by page with the original.

  3. 3

    I attach the notarial certificate: "I certify that this is a true and correct copy of a record in the possession of [your name]", with my signature and seal.

  4. 4

    It is recorded in my notary journal, as Colorado law requires.

Certified Copy FAQ

Only if it was issued by another state. A Colorado notary cannot certify copies of Colorado birth, death, marriage or divorce certificates; order a certified copy from Colorado Vital Records or your county instead.

No. A Colorado notary cannot certify that someone is alive or certify other facts. If the requesting agency accepts it, the person can sign a sworn statement in front of me and I notarize the signature (a jurat). Ask the agency first which format it accepts.

$15 per certified copy, the Colorado maximum for a notarial act, plus the travel fee if I come to you. If we meet at a community location (Tienda Salvadoreña, MSU Denver, or any Denver Public Library branch), it’s $10 per copy and no travel fee.

Yes. I must see the original and make or supervise the copy myself. I cannot certify a copy of a copy, a fax, or a scan.

Yes. Passports, driver’s licenses and ID cards can be certified as long as the document does not prohibit copying. The receiving agency decides whether it accepts a notarized copy, so check with them first.

For birth, marriage and death records, no: the Colorado Secretary of State requires a certified copy from the issuing office. For other documents, ask the receiving country or agency first. See my apostille requirements checklist. Requirements checklist.
